title: Balancing equations
examples: How do I know which atoms to start balancing first?
What does the coefficient actually represent in the equation?
Can I use atoms instead of coefficients in the final answer?

explain.say: Today we are learning how to balance chemical equations.

items: Reactants are on the left side.
Products are on the right side.

explain.say: The first rule is conservation of atoms.
We balance by placing whole numbers called coefficients.
State symbols tell us the physical state of matter.
Consider the formation of water from hydrogen and oxygen.
In the real world, burning methane gas in oxygen is a reaction.

faq.q: Do I have to balance every single equation I see?
faq.a: You only need to balance equations when the question specifically asks you to do so.

faq.q: Can I change the chemical formulas while balancing?
faq.a: No, you must keep the chemical formulas exactly as they are given in the problem.
asks: Should I change the names of the elements?

faq.q: What does a coefficient mean in the equation?
faq.a: A coefficient tells you the number of molecules or moles of a substance involved.
asks: What is the purpose of the big numbers?
Do the coefficients change the substance?

faq.q: Does the state symbol change when I balance the equation?
faq.a: No, the state symbols stay the same throughout the process of balancing the equation.
asks: Do I write the state symbols again?
Are the states important for balancing?

faq.q: If I use the wrong coefficient, what happens?
faq.a: If you use the wrong coefficient, the number of atoms on both sides will not match up.
asks: How do I know if I am wrong?
What is the first thing to check?

facts: The law of conservation of mass states that atoms are neither created nor destroyed.
Coefficients are the whole numbers placed in front of the chemical formulas.
State symbols indicate the physical state: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous.
Balancing equations ensures the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides.

quiz.say: Balance the reaction: Fe(s) + Cl₂(g) → FeCl₃(s)
quiz.why: You need two iron atoms on the left side to match the two iron atoms on the right side.

wrong.0: This would put too many atoms on the left side compared to the right.
wrong.2: This leaves one chlorine atom unbalanced on the left side.
wrong.3: Using three iron atoms would create too many iron atoms on the left.

quiz.say: Balance the reaction: C₂(g) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + H₂O(g)
quiz.why: You need two molecules of water on the right side to balance the two carbon atoms on the left.

wrong.1: This leaves two oxygen atoms unbalanced on the right side.
wrong.2: This would create too many oxygen atoms on the right side.
wrong.3: This does not account for the two carbon atoms on the left side.

quiz.say: If you have 3 molecules of N₂ and 3 molecules of H₂ reacting to form NH₃, what is the correct equation?
quiz.why: You need three molecules of hydrogen to ensure three nitrogen atoms are available for the product.

wrong.0: Using two molecules of hydrogen leaves one nitrogen atom unbalanced.
wrong.1: This would use too many hydrogen molecules compared to the nitrogen.
wrong.2: This uses too many atoms overall, violating conservation.
